arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation users (hikers, climbers) and (B) Emergency preparedness organizations (SAR agencies, NGOs). Each participant views a product description of the 406 MHz distress beacon, highlighting its reliability in remote environments and interoperability (for T1) or its standardized, interoperable distress capability (for T2). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this beacon at a price of $300-500?" (binary yes/no).
arguments.sample: 200 participants: 100 from outdoor recreation forums/clubs (representing T1) and 100 from emergency preparedness forums/NGOs (representing T2). Recruit via targeted ads to ensure geographic diversity.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) for each participant group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency preparedness participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).

arguments.decision_rule: If both groups achieve purchase intent rates ≥40%, both theories are considered supported. If only one group achieves the threshold, that theory is considered more likely. If neither group achieves the threshold, both theories are considered unlikely.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited public information on ACR’s current consumer reach and sales channels.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must be from sources published on or before late 2002; later developments are not usable.
Financial data for ACR is not available in the dossier.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/industrial product line into new segments (e.g., commercial fishing, recreational boating) without creating a distinct consumer proposition.
3) Maintain the current product portfolio and not pursue a new consumer offering (no expansion).

T1.who_benefits: Hikers, climbers, and other outdoor users who need a safety device that can be used in life-threatening situations.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These users currently rely on mobile phones, radio, or satellite phones, but these can be damaged, lost, or out of range. A distress beacon offers a redundant, automatic alert that can be activated without user intervention.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online, capturing the full retail price. The company also benefits from recurring revenue through rental or maintenance contracts.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. remain stable or grow in 2002.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety devices that work in remote environments.
Distribution channels (retailers, online) can reach this demographic.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation participants will indicate a willingness to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $300-500.
Sales of the beacon will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor activity (e.g., national parks, mountain ranges).

Interoperability is a critical requirement for SAR agencies.
Price sensitivity is lower for public sector buyers compared to consumer markets.

X1.name: Consumer vs Government Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation users (hikers, climbers) and (B) Emergency preparedness organizations (SAR agencies, NGOs). Each participant views a product description of the 406 MHz distress beacon, highlighting its reliability in remote environments and interoperability (for T1) or its standardized, interoperable distress capability (for T2). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this beacon at a price of $300-500?" (binary yes/no).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 from outdoor recreation forums/clubs (representing T1) and 100 from emergency preparedness forums/NGOs (representing T2). Recruit via targeted ads to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) for each participant group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency preparedness participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).

X1.decision_rule: If both groups achieve purchase intent rates ≥40%, both theories are considered supported. If only one group achieves the threshold, that theory is considered more likely. If neither group achieves the threshold, both theories are considered unlikely.

final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation users (hikers, climbers) who need a reliable emergency backup in remote areas.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that provides automatic, redundant alerting in remote environments, leveraging the existing FCC registration and interoperability standards to ensure safety and compliance.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Government Purchase Intent Test as outlined.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 (outdoor recreation demand) and T2 (emergency preparedness demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of consumer purchase intent or willingness to pay in 2002.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent rates ≥40% for outdoor recreation participants, T1 would become likely and the recommendation would shift toward developing a consumer product.
If the test shows purchase intent rates ≥40% for emergency preparedness participants, T2 would become likely and the recommendation would shift toward pursuing a government/SAR market.

Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation users (hikers, climbers) and (B) Emergency preparedness organizations (SAR agencies, NGOs). Each participant views a product description of the 406 MHz distress beacon, highlighting its reliability in remote environments and interoperability (for T1) or its standardized, interoperable distress capability (for T2). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this beacon at a price of $300-500?" (binary yes/no).
arguments.sample: 200 participants: 100 from outdoor recreation forums/clubs (representing T1) and 100 from emergency preparedness forums/NGOs (representing T2). Recruit via targeted ads to ensure geographic diversity.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) for each participant group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency preparedness participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).

arguments.decision_rule: If both groups achieve purchase intent rates ≥40%, both theories are considered supported. If only one group achieves the threshold, that theory is considered more likely. If neither group achieves the threshold, both theories are considered unlikely.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness) using the 406 MHz distress-beacon technology.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation users (hikers, climbers) and (B) Emergency preparedness organizations (SAR agencies, NGOs). Each participant views a product description of the 406 MHz distress beacon, highlighting its reliability in remote environments and interoperability (for T1) or its standardized, interoperable distress capability (for T2). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this beacon at a price of $300-500?" (binary yes/no).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 from outdoor recreation forums/clubs (representing T1) and 100 from emergency preparedness forums/NGOs (representing T2). Recruit via targeted ads to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) for each participant group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreation participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency preparedness participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).

X1.decision_rule: If both groups achieve purchase intent rates ≥40%, both theories are considered supported. If only one group achieves the threshold, that theory is considered more likely. If neither group achieves the threshold, both theories are considered unlikely.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or adoption behavior for the 406 MHz distress beacon. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Government Purchase Intent Test (200 participants, €18,000, 10 weeks) to gather real purchase intent data before any investment. The test will clarify whether outdoor recreation users are willing to adopt the beacon at the proposed price point, which is essential for justifying a differentiated consumer product line. Until then

final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Government Purchase Intent Test as outlined.

X1.name: Price vs Prestige Messaging Test
X1.method: Randomized controlled online survey with two parallel groups. Group A sees a low-price, functional description of a lawn tractor (cost-effectiveness message). Group B sees a high-price, design-focused description emphasizing status and modern lifestyle (prestige message). Both groups are asked about purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and willingness to pay a fixed price. The test also collects demographic data (age, household income, home ownership status).
X1.sample: 200 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age and income brackets. 100 per group.
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) and average willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A’s average purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher than Group B’s, because cost-effectiveness drives demand.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B’s average purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher than Group A’s, because status and prestige motivate buyers.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s average willingness to pay exceeds Group B’s by at least €100 and its purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher on the 1‑10 scale, then T1 is supported. position.recommendation: Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically compare homeowner willingness to pay for a branded John Deere lawn tractor versus a generic model. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching individual buyers.
Must consider existing dealer network and any existing consumer products.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, home gardening, or a niche industrial application).
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B markets and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.

Dealer network can reach individual buyers effectively.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lawn Tractor Buyers
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a generic lawn tractor and a branded John Deere tractor with identical specs. They are asked: "How much would you pay for this lawn tractor?" (open numeric response). They also rate perceived time‑saving benefit (1‑10 scale) and perceived prestige/status (1‑10 scale).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults aged 35‑65, recruited via an online panel to reflect suburban/urban mix and gender balance.
X1.measure: Average willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) for each tractor; difference in WTP between generic and branded John Deere; correlation between WTP and prestige/status rating.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average WTP for branded John Deere will be at least 1.5x higher than for generic tractor, and the prestige/status rating will be positively correlated with WTP.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP for branded John Deere will be at least 1.2x higher than for generic tractor, and the prestige/status rating will be strongly positively correlated with WTP.

final.target_customer: Homeowners in suburban and urban areas who maintain small gardens and are considering purchasing a lawn tractor.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes the lawn tractor’s time‑saving benefits and reliability, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network to reach individual buyers.
final.next_action: Run the online willingness‑to‑pay survey with 500 participants, collect open numeric willingness‑to‑pay amounts and prestige‑status ratings, and analyze the difference in average WTP between branded John Deere and generic tractor.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to a single independent source (deere-wheelhorse-demand) that supports T1; no direct evidence on homeowner willingness to pay a premium for brand prestige exists. The test will resolve this uncertainty.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a generic lawn tractor and a branded John Deere tractor with identical specs. X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a 1962‑era lawn tractor (specifications, price, and a brief description emphasizing either time‑saving/convenience or status/modern lifestyle). They are asked: "How much would you be willing to pay for this tractor?" (open‑ended). They also rate the tractor on a 1‑10 scale for perceived time‑saving (1‑
X1.sample: 500 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region (suburban vs urban).
X1.measure: Average willingness‑to‑pay (EUR) for the time‑saving description versus the status description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average willingness‑to‑pay will be higher for the time‑saving description than for the status description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average willingness‑to‑pay will be higher for the status description than for the time‑saving description.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness‑to‑pay for the time‑saving description exceeds the average for the status description by at least €150 (a 20% premium), we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status description exceeds the time‑saving description by at least €150, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than €150, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address homeowner motivations for lawn tractors. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed homeowner survey test (X1) to compare willingness to pay for time‑saving versus status messaging. If the test shows a €150 premium for the time‑saving description, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting time‑saving homeowners; otherwise, maintain focus on existing B2B markets and dealer network.
final.target_customer: Homeowners in suburban areas who view lawn care as a time‑saving, convenient chore and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and ease of use.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor offering superior time‑saving performance, built‑in accessories, and a premium brand promise, sold through existing dealer network with training to highlight convenience benefits.
final.next_action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 homeowner survey test (X1) to measure willingness to pay for time‑saving versus status messaging.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to a single independent source (deere-wheelhorse-demand) that supports T1. No direct evidence of homeowner willingness to pay a premium for time‑saving features exists. The test is needed to resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows a €150 premium for the status description, we would shift focus to a status‑driven proposition.
If the test shows no significant premium for either description, we would recommend no expansion and maintain the existing dealer model.
